scenes.headline: How token-level RL stands in for the real reward
scenes.sub: A first-order approximation, two gaps, and the tricks that close them.
scenes.say: Hi, I'm Qubit! Reasoning models are rewarded per answer but trained per token. Here's why that works, and when it breaks.

scenes.text: Token-level RL is a first-order approximation to the true sequence-level reward. It holds only while two gaps stay small.
scenes.say: The idea: the token-level objective is a first-order approximation to the true reward. It holds only while two gaps stay small.

scenes.title: A product, cut down to a sum
scenes.say: Each token's ratio, new policy over old, is one plus a small delta.

parts.note: the true sequence ratio: every token ratio multiplied
parts.say: The true sequence ratio multiplies hundreds of them. Correct, but numerically hopeless.

parts.note: the token-level surrogate: just the sum
parts.say: To first order, that product is one plus the sum. And the sum is the token-level objective.

parts.note: the cross terms the surrogate throws away
parts.say: It drops only the cross terms: tiny while the ratios hug one, large when they drift.

scenes.title: Where the two gaps come from

steps.say: A fast inference engine samples the responses.
A separate training engine scores them again. Different kernels give slightly different probabilities: the training–inference discrepancy.
Several mini-batch updates follow, so later batches meet a policy that has already drifted: policy staleness.

steps.note: IS weight corrects gap one; clipping caps gap two
steps.say: The importance weight corrects the first gap; it is the first-order term itself. Clipping caps the second.

scenes.label: steps until on-policy training collapses without the training–inference IS correction
scenes.note: KL spikes and entropy craters first
scenes.say: Remove that importance correction and on-policy training collapses within about a hundred and fifty steps.

left.title: Routing left free
items: The two engines can pick different experts
The ratio compares two different subnetworks
left.say: In a mixture of experts, the engines can route a token to different experts. The ratio then compares two subnetworks.

right.title: Routing Replay
items: Pin the routed experts during optimization
One fixed subnetwork, optimized like a dense model
Restores the ratio, but biases the target policy
right.say: Routing Replay pins the routed experts, so the ratio means something again. The price is a biased target policy.

scenes.text: IS correction, clipping and Routing Replay are one move: keep token ratios near one, so the approximation holds.
scenes.say: Importance weights, clipping and Routing Replay are one move: keep the ratios near one, so the approximation holds.

recap: Token-level RL is the sum; the reward, the product
Two gaps: engine discrepancy and policy staleness
Routing Replay pins MoE experts, at a bias
scenes.say: To recap: the sum stands in for the product, two gaps threaten it, and three tricks close them.
